title: Notes of Ministry - 77 - April 1979

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 77 - April 1979 (2489)/Notes of Ministry - 77 - April - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I desire, beloved brethren, to speak of spiritual instruction in view of what has already engaged us in our gatherings. The Lord saw fit to call attention to it in every reading and it seems to underline the great importance of being instructed, not only in the sense of acquired knowledge but being instructed in virtue of your link with the Lord Jesus and your link with the Holy Spirit, and thus, as being instructed, you will be competent to have your part in the building, in the building up of what is for the divine pleasure. As we have been often taught, the first and second epistles to Timothy are to instruct him to know how to behave himself in God’s house, it says, “which is ... the pillar and base of the truth”, 1 Timothy 3: 15. Paul was at great pains to instruct his young disciple in the matters that were relevant to the testimony, and one feels it is a situation of the utmost need at the moment that the brethren should be divinely instructed and that room should be made in the ordering of our lives too, and the apportioning of our time, so that we are instructed in the things of God and able to give help.

This scripture in Isaiah is one that affects me very much as it is an allusion to the Lord Jesus Himself personally. That He should thus speak prophetically, that He should speak as an instructed One, is of profound interest. When you ponder the greatness and the glory of His Person? His word giving effect even to creation, that as Man here in dependence He should take the place of being an instructed Person is wonderful. It is one of those touches in the Scriptures which bow your spirit in holy adoration as you think of the perfection of that manhood, so normal, so perfect in its advancing stages; day by day He took the place of an instructed Person. It says, “Jehovah hath given me the tongue of the instructed, that I should know how to succour by a word him that is weary”.

We spoke earlier today of feet washing, how that word ‘succour’ enters into the service of feet washing, and how we can only do it as instructed by God to give a word to him that is weary, to minister refreshment to a weary soul. So the Lord Jesus served thus. Think of Him drawing near to those two on the road to Emmaus, those weary souls as they wended their way away from the divine centre, and in His condescending grace He moved towards them and spoke a word to those that were weary. What a touch! The word of His grace. Luke’s gospel in all its richness setting out that thought. So we should go after weary persons. How many of them are amongst us, weary of the way they have come, in exercise of heart and needing a word of instruction, needing a word that has come from the Lord Himself and from God Himself.
It says, “He wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear to hear as the instructed”.

We recall what has been said about this that even the Lord was wakened out of His sleep by the Father. In the morning He was wakened, not so to speak by the natural movements of His body as having rested, but He was wakened by the Father each day, and His ear was wakened to listen to the divine instruction that was required for that day. What a picture of perfect dependence!

Beloved brethren, are we dependent enough? are we dependent enough each day? are we dependent enough as we approach the gatherings of the saints? I feel that if we were more dependent in our links with God we would prove help to a greater degree than we do. There is nothing so devitalising in a spiritual sense than to be self-sufficient; as believers in our pathway here nothing should be undertaken without absolute and constant dependence on God. We should be simple about these things. We tend to take only matters of moment to God, only matters of burden and deep crisis, but the essence of spiritual life is that a believer takes even the simplest matters to the Father. It betokens that attitude in which your ear is wakened morning by morning to hear as an instructed person. I say this to younger brethren because of the complexities of business life and the need for direction. How often we enter into situations naturally feeling able for them. We should not enter into any situation except in utter dependence on God that He will help us to keep in the path of His will. Every move you make, even household-wise, every move you make in your employment, every action you take in relation to the Lord’s interest in a place, never do it except in absolute dependence on God because, in doing it that way, you are like the Lord Jesus Himself, and what greater example could we have than the Lord Jesus as a Man here? He moved that way day by day in everything. And that way God will bless you and help you in your movements.

In Proverbs it says, “Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father, and attend to know intelligence; for I give you good doctrine—forsake ye not my law”. Every believer should read the book of Proverbs as part of his constant daily reading. The book of Proverbs is one of the outstanding books of Scripture for moral instruction, because, after all, everything that occurs in the life of a believer has a moral bearing. A believer’s life is not entirely related to what is material and circumstantial; a believer’s life as under the Father and as under Christ and under the Spirit has a moral bearing and he needs the instruction of the book of Proverbs by the Spirit, not in the sense of a legal precept, but by the Spirit, for wisdom. So it says, “Hear, ye children, the instruction of a father”. Thank God, beloved brethren, for the fathers amongst us. I do not say exactly, although it might be synonymous, Thank God for older persons. I say, Thank God for the fathers and for the instruction that they can give us in the way of wisdom and experience in the things of God, and let us increasingly value the spirit of fatherhood amongst us. This young man says, “I was a son unto my father”. He did not say, “I was a son of my father”; he said, “I was a son unto my father”.

Are all the younger brethren in this room at this time sons unto their father? Can your spiritual fathers and your natural fathers look upon you and say, You are a son unto me? One of the great needs of the moment is a spirit of confidence between older men and younger men both naturally and spiritually. I think it is something that the Spirit of God is pressing that there should be the spirit of absolute trust, that older persons mean what they say and say what they mean, and that younger persons can have confidence in them in that way so that the glorious features of sonship come out. What is sonship? Sonship in effect is just this matter of holy confidence and love in that relationship between a father and a son. So the book of Proverbs gives you the counsel and the instruction of a father in regard to all these things, and not only in delivering you from the morass of evil as depicted in the case of the wicked woman but also in regard to the glory of wisdom’s house. And that is a fine thought, beloved brethren, that the path of instruction leads you to wisdom’s house which has been built; it is on its seven pillars and is established there in glory and blessing for men, that which is greater than, and outside, everything that this world can give.

We should be exercised to testify and to demonstrate that what obtains in the christian circle is in its quality, and in its power, and in its moral excellence greater than any attraction that this world can afford to our young people. The spirit amongst the brethren, the demonstration of unity and grace, the evidence of life and vitality, the fact that persons love the Lord and do not love the world, that their walk and their ways are in accord with the truth, these things, beloved brethren, are a demonstration to our young people that wisdom’s house in its moral excellence is greater than anything that this world can offer. Instruction comes that way, and it comes in Proverbs, as we have been taught, in the way of influence and headship. Proverbs is a book of headship. Proverbs is not a book of lordship. Proverbs is a book of headship in which things flow in a reciprocal way amongst God’s people on the line of influence through fatherhood towards sons. We value our young people. We pray to God constantly that not another one of them will be lost. We should, search ourselves, brethren, in the presence of God day by day as to our responsibility to our younger brethren and that it could never at the judgment seat be laid to our charge that we in any way diverted them because we did not demonstrate the features of fatherhood and and the instruction that was connected with wisdom’s house.

In Timothy it says, “My child, be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus. And the things thou hast heard of me in the presence of many witnesses, these entrust to faithful men, such as shall be competent to instruct others also”. There is a great need for instruction in fundamental things. I would like to speak in a friendly way to my younger brethren, and I trust I will not be accused of being too intellectual, but there are certain matters I would like to raise with you as to whether, as a young believer, you are instructed. Are you instructed as to the cardinal difference between the Old and the New Testaments? Does every young man in this room know that, as to the cardinal difference between the Old and the New Testament? Does every young man know the difference between the three synoptic gospels and John’s gospel? Does every young person know the difference between the rapture and the appearing? Does every young person know the difference between the wilderness and the land as related to the Lord’s supper? You know, brethren, I could go on and on and on; but if the work of God and the teaching according to the truth are to prosper amongst us, the younger brethren will have to be instructed constantly in regard to these matters.

I was preaching on an occasion and I made reference to the rapture, and a young person said to me that she had never heard of that in her life—in a christian household and she had never heard of the rapture! I trust I am saying this in the right spirit, beloved brethren; it may be I am not giving the younger brethren sufficient credit, but I can see that unless these great and salient points of teaching in the Scriptures are understood, the workmen will be inefficient, These things are acquired by personal experience in the power of the Spirit with the Lord Himself; not merely in the acquirement of the facts mentally but gone through with the Lord so that you know what they mean as related to the great spiritual order of things of which Christ is the centre.

In regard to Acts 18, here are two of Solomon’s workmen with a piece of timber from Lebanon, a man “mighty in the scriptures”. Beloved brethren, do we read the Scriptures sufficiently? Do we read the Scriptures as food for our souls? How good to use the living word of God to feed your affections with Christ, to ponder over the holy words, the holy record of Christ, and let your spirit worship as you ponder. Have you ever read the word of God and the depth and the power have so affected your soul that you bowed your head in worship? Apollos was eloquent in the Scriptures. There is no power in ministry, nor in preaching, nor is there real power to build without instruction in the Scriptures. A brother in the reading referred to the morning reading of the Scriptures. We did not touch on it yesterday, but in the ark that Noah built there was a window and it gave light from heaven.

Every household should have a window, and that window is the daily reading of the Scriptures; it is the responsibility of the head of the house to bring continually the light of God onto the household situation.

Oh how adoringly we should read the Holy Scriptures! Our heart should exult in the counsels and the purposes of God as they are expressed in the Holy Scriptures, the magnitude and the greatness of these thoughts of His. What a treasure we have in the word of God! It is the one book which multiplies its circulation year by year as the hungry souls of men and women thirst for the living word of

God. What for? Just to make them better acquainted with doctrine? No, but to feed their souls, to feed their affections in regard to the glorious Person of whom they speak, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.

So Aquila and Priscilla heard of Apollos and took him to them and unfolded to him the way of God more exactly. They saw the great potentiality in such material for the house, and there is the suggestion of workmanship in that they “took him to them and unfolded to him the way of God more exactly”. In other words, they gave him instruction in regard to the great truth of the assembly, the great truth of what God had wrought in Christ, raised from the dead and ascended to His own place in glory, and the Spirit down here. These things give us enlargement as to the glory and greatness of the dispensation in which we are found; how much greater by far it is than anything that preceded it, and greater by far than the day to come. Mr. Darby said that the moral greatness of David dancing before the ark exceeded the millennial glory of Solomon on his brazen scaffold (‘Synopsis’ Vol.1 p.358). What a thought that is, that in its moral sense the present time and what is connected with the working out of God’s thoughts in relation to Christ is greater than the day of display. The Spirit of God would instruct us more exactly as to these great matters connected with the present time so that we are more serviceable in the work of the Lord.

articles.title: THE KINGDOM OF GOD COME IN POWER
articles.author: A. B. Parker
articles.place: Word in meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: It has occurred to me that Mark’s reference to the mount of transfiguration is like a psalm.

Matthew tells us that the Lord Jesus said, “There are some of those standing here that shall not taste of death at all until they shall have seen the Son of man coming in his kingdom”, Matthew 16: 28. Luke tells us that the Lord Jesus said, “There are some of those standing here who shall not taste death until they shall have seen the kingdom of God”, Luke 9: 27.

Mark’s account is, “There are some of those standing here that shall not taste death until they shall have seen the kingdom of God come in power”. The point Mark makes is that the kingdom of God has come—come in power. Mark’s experience was witness to the fact that the kingdom of God had come in power; its power had recovered him.

It would seem that Mark was a young man with pure motives. It would seem that he had been sheltered in a godly home—that he was a choice young man. I suggest that his motives were pure, based on his remarks about the young man that followed Jesus when He was apprehended, with a linen cloth cast about his naked body. It would seem that he was referring to himself, figuratively. The linen cloth would suggest that his manner of life was pure and his going with Barnabas and Saul would be with pure motives, but he lacked in definite committal to discipleship. The cloth was soon snatched away. But later in his gospel he refers to a young man in the torch clothed in white. Much soul history would be experienced in between.

The kingdom of God became a very special subject with Mark after he was recovered. He realised that he had not been a very good subject of the kingdom. He had been weak in the day of battle. When the enemy’s power showed itself in the false prophet Bar-jesus, he went back from the conflict to Jerusalem, to a sphere of shelter and care. Nevertheless, God had His eye upon him and in some way Mark was recovered, and the Holy Spirit would use his experience in failure to develop an appreciation of the perfect service of Christ. Later, as we know, Paul could tell Timothy to take Mark and bring him, for he was serviceable to Paul for ministry (2 Timothy 4: 11). Elsewhere he tells us that Mark was one of a few who had been a consolation to him as fellow-workers for the kingdom of God (Colossians 4: 10, 11). So we are not surprised that in his gospel he makes much of the kingdom of God, telling us that it was seen as “come in power”. And his recovery was a witness to this.

Dear brethren, our ministry takes on power when we can witness to what we minister. Mark was a witness to the fact that the kingdom of God had come in power. The kingdom is not in outward manifestation as yet; it is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit and we are to be witness to it because the Holy Spirit still is here. The kingdom of God relates peculiarly to the power and operation of the Holy. Spirit sent from heaven.

Mark was not one of those who were with Jesus on the mount. The writers of the synoptic gospels recorded what they were told as to that occasion. It is right to minister what we learn from others, but we need to appropriate it so that it becomes our own, and power in such ministry comes as we go through things experimentally. So when Mark describes the transfiguration scene he tells us that Elias was there, with Moses. The other writers say Moses and Elias, but Mark names Elias first for Elias peculiarly represents the kingdom of God come in recovering power—the power of recovery in the prophetic word. So, dear brethren, we want increasingly to value this character of meeting, to appreciate its possibilities. Mark would tell us that if we want to see the kingdom of God come in power, put proper appreciation on the prophetic word—give it the place to which it is entitled. It is not greater than the ministry of Moses, for Moses was the apostle, but Elias was, outstandingly, the prophet. The kingdom of God come in power in this day of recovery relates peculiarly to God’s voice being heard through the prophets.

2 Samuel 9: 1–13; 19: 24–These are familiar passages of Scripture that have often been preached from, but can afford to be preached from again, because souls who have savoured what divine mercy and goodness are never tire of hearing the recounting of God’s ways with His people. We are told earlier on in the book that David waxed stronger and stronger but the house of Saul became continually weaker. We can be thankful when that
is so, for it means that Christ is having His place in our hearts and the flesh is having less place. It says in Galatians, “The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh”

(Galatians 5: 17). It does not say, ‘The Spirit lusts against the flesh’, because you cannot associate lust with the Spirit; but the Spirit is against the flesh. In that section we find what the works of the flesh are and what the fruit of the Spirit is, and there is a very sharp contrast.
So if the house of David is waxing stronger and stronger, we can rejoice, for it must necessarily be that the house of Saul must wax weaker and weaker.

So here was one of the house of Saul, and no doubt he would have his reflections as to the history. His father, Jonathan, had been a lover of David. Maybe, if Mephibosheth was old enough, his father would have spoken well to him of David. Heaven did not lose sight of the fact that Jonathan loved David. Heaven will never lose sight of the fact if there is any response, whatever it is, to divine acts of mercy and grace.

Mr. Raven said a remarkable thing: ‘If a man has the smallest appreciation of Christ—let it be as small as may be—that man is ‘made meet’’ (N.S. Vol.3. p.26). How that opens up what God is in His magnanimity and His power to treasure and carry through even the very slightest appreciation of Christ. God will let nothing of Christ fall to the ground; He will let nothing of Christ disappear; anything that is truly of Christ will be carried right through into the sphere where all that is of God will shine eternally. That is a matter of tremendous comfort to me. You think of persons who have been bright and who have fallen away. I am thinking of a man who was once a bright christian and fell away. He did not become a wicked man, but he stopped going to meetings and he had habits that are not becoming to a christian. Then he died very suddenly. Well, nothing of Christ that was in that man will ever be lost. This is not to put any premium on failure, or give any excuse for anyone to go away, but it is a wonderful thing that the Lord knows them that are His and He is able to bring through every little bit of the heart’s appreciation of Christ and of the goodness of God.

One of the subtle and dangerous things of the present time is that God seemingly has a recognition among certain people, but there is a passing by of Christ. Beware in what you read or listen to of anything that will exalt God and give Him a certain place but ignores Christ. Everything that is of value to God centres in Christ and if in anything He has not His rightful place let us beware of it. God has made Him both Lord and Christ and there is none other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved. If it is a matter of approach to the Father, Christ Himself said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father unless by me”, John 14: 6.

God is faithful; God remembers things. He remembers the best part of the history of Israel. In the prophets we are reminded that God remembered things for them, remembered when they went after Him in the wilderness. God never forgets the best times that we have had. So this fact that Mephibosheth’s father had loved David was an advantage to this man away down there in Lodebar, a name which means ‘no pasture, a dry place, a far-away place’. He might, as Jonathan’s son, have expected to be in the king’s house, having the best of everything, but he was in a place with no pasture, remote from the centre of blessing.

Yet God had His eye upon him and He used His beloved, His servant David, to express that. David had feelings sympathetic with those of God. He says, “I will certainly show thee kindness for Jonathan thy father’s sake”, but when he makes enquiry of Ziba he says, “If I may show the kindness of God to him”, the kindness of God. David was sympathetic with divine thoughts, he reflected the feelings of God, and he says, “Is there anybody?” Think of God looking around and saying, “Is there anybody?” I am sure that there will be recoveries and there will be movements of heart. Why? Maybe because of a link with the testimony that someone has. We sometimes find that; we hear that So-and-so’s son, or So-and-so’s widow, is interested. Why? In one sense because of their connections with the testimony, though God is able to work at any time, anywhere, with anyone—and let us be prepared for it.

So David sent for him—“Fetch him”. I can imagine this messenger coming to Mephibosheth. It may well have been that Mephibosheth trembled. ‘Is he going to do what he did to those other people? Am I to die? Why is he sending for me?’ Well, he soon found out. The very first thing that David did when Mephibosheth came, possibly trembling, into his presence was to set him at rest. “Fear not; for I will certainly shew thee kindness for Jonathan thy father’s sake, and will restore thee all the land of Saul thy father; and thou shalt eat bread at my table continually”. David maintained in his ascendancy the grace that marked him in his rejection. The Lord is the same in glory as He was when here on earth; there is no change in His disposition, no change in His power to overcome by His grace; and His love is still the same—“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, and today, and to the ages to come”, Hebrews 13: 8. He is able and ready at all times to exhibit the perfection of the divine disposition of grace and mercy towards poor fallen man—the character of God.

There is coming a time when the ways of God will change. His character will not change; His attributes will not change; but there is a time of judgment coming. It must be so; the Scriptures give plain declaration of that. God is able with infinite accuracy to deal with every situation and every person in perfect righteousness. But it is wonderful to think of the way in which grace and forgiveness are now being extended to those who have not merited them.

So here is Mephibosheth; at a stroke his circumstances have changed; things have taken on another aspect altogether. That is just like conversion. You go through the gospels and you find how many people had just one transaction with the Lord and from that time things were completely different. We come to meetings and it very often takes a long time before we yield to divine grace. Nevertheless, that has not changed the way God has acted; it has not changed His patience; it only brings out and glorifies the way God in patience and in grace carries on with His work.

The passage in 2 Samuel 19 shows that Mephibosheth had been deceived by his servant Ziba who had conveyed to David that Mephibosheth was not grateful for David’s intervention (see 2 Samuel 16). Nevertheless Mephibosheth manifests the working of grace. He had received not only a place at David’s table which in his own mind no doubt was the greatest thing—but he had received Saul’s land. He had been given servants and these servants were commissioned to till the land and bring forth the fruits of it. So Mephibosheth in a certain sense was independent. But that was nothing compared with the grace that had
affected his soul in that he was to eat bread continually at the king’s table.
So David is mollified to a certain extent and says, “Thou and Ziba divide the land”.

Mephibosheth just got half his former possessions; he had his inheritance reduced. But Mephibosheth was not concerned about that. He would say, ‘Let him take the lot. As long as I have a place at your table the rest can go by the board’. The apostle Paul, speaking of the Lord Jesus Christ, says, “On account of whom I have suffered the loss of all”, Philippians 3: 8. Oh, a true Mephibosheth was the apostle, and naturally he had had a good deal to boast of.
He says, “I count also all things to be loss, on account of the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord”, Philippians 3: 8. Wonderful language!

Oh let us have hearts that are appreciative of the grace that has taken us up and given us a place at the King’s table. That is worth more than anything else, dear brethren; it is the fellowship of God’s Son Jesus Christ our Lord; that is one of the greatest privileges that we can have. If we lose everything else here, if we have that, it is something to rejoice in. Let us be more appreciative and able to discriminate as to what our true blessings are. Any loss that we might have does not count in comparison. There will be loss; there is loss, and there will possibly be more. Things are getting very difficult; we feel for the younger generation.

Things in the world are closing up, but we have this confidence, that God will make a way through and that as you esteem the Lord Jesus, and the testimony and the fellowship have the first place. God will see to the rest. We are not promised fortunes, we are not promised the best of everything, but if we have Christ, as one in poverty could say, ‘What want I more?’ It will be worth it, brethren;

it will be worth it, young people; make your resolution that whatever happens you will stay by David’s table, to appreciate the fellowship and appreciate the grace that has given you a place in the divine presence where there is peace and rest. Amen.

I am thinking, beloved brethren, of the need for manhood. Some of us were impressed recently with the way that God has set out the glory and greatness of His ways with men in the Man Christ Jesus, and that manhood according to God’s mind is seen in Him. We, as having part in the testimony currently, should be exercised to be expressive of that order of manhood and it is interesting to note the references to manhood throughout Scripture. What has come into my heart recently is this expression as to “the mighty men whom David had”, and the way that three of them are mentioned as working together.

What our brother has just mentioned as to standing would be a feature of manhood, standing upright. God made man upright (Ecclesiastes 7: 29), and there is a need to be upright as to righteousness, and upright in our thoughts of one another, so that there is transparency. That is a feature of manhood, so that a man does not have to hide what he has done; it is open for all to see. It is beautiful to see the way that the Lord Jesus Himself moved in this scene and the things that He did, and then when you come to the end of the gospel of John you get that expression, “Behold the man” (John 19: 5). While it came from the lips of one who did not shine in the feature of manhood, yet his testimony was right. What a Man Jesus is! What a Man He was in His pathway here, and the glory and greatness of the features of manhood set out in Him go through eternally. It is that order of manhood that we are to have part in. Having part in the testimony currently involves manhood. You get that word in 1 Corinthians 16: 13, “Quit yourselves like men”. There is need for strength in that regard, to quit ourselves like men and be strong. That marked these men of David and it is interesting that it says, “These are the names of the mighty men whom David had”. The list goes on, bringing out the qualities of these men, and their exploits, and it comes down all the way to Uriah the Hittite. Each has his distinctive place as protecting what was precious in David’s time.

As to Solomon’s palanquin it is said, “Threescore mighty men are about it”, Song of Solomon 3: 7. It is that quality of preparedness, as it says here, “at the risk of their lives”. I believe that is what the current testimonial position demands of us, preparedness to go at the risk of our lives. It is a quality that is needed, and it is a quality that has not marked us very much; but in view of the power of the enemy showing itself as it has, and continues to do, there is need of this preparedness to set ourselves, even at the risk of our lives. It is a solemn thing to consider, and it involves the sisterhood, as Esther said, “If I perish, I perish”. Her part in the testimony demanded a full surrender, and that marked these men. It is beautiful the way it is brought out, “These are the names of the mighty men whom David had”. He had such men, and the Lord Jesus is looking for such men. There is, a reference as the Lord speaks to the Father to “the men whom thou gavest me” (John 17: 6), an expression that we do well to think of as showing the feelings that the Lord had for those that were near Him and faithful to Him. Things are the same today. We would have an assurance in our souls of His delight in what is near to Him. I think we sensed it on Lord’s day morning. It is a precious matter to be near Him; it brings out liberty and freedom in expression from the hearts of one and another who are consciously near Him.

These men who broke through in David’s time were near enough to sense the longings of David, the desire of his heart. There must have been a unison in the way they acted as they did, breaking through the camp of the Philistines to draw water out of the well of Bethlehem.

And in bringing it back the precious thought is that what they did contributed to the service of God. That is a feature of manhood, to enter into what is Godward. We are not thinking of ourselves. I believe that it is a feature of manhood to consider for the heart of Christ, and to consider for what is not our own but for Him who has enlisted us in this time of exercise that the testimony currently involves. So David’s men broke through; they provided for David what he longed for, “however he would not drink of it, but poured it out to Jehovah. And he said, Be it far from me, Jehovah, that I should do this thing!” He puts a true valuation on what had been secured; he would not take it as for himself. The breaking through at the risk of their lives was something more than what was for his own heart; it involved what was for the heart of God. Such are the times in which we are, times in which what is being secured is for the heart of God. What is for the heart of our Lord Jesus Christ is for the Father’s heart, involving the

preciousness of the service of God. We need to think increasingly of the service of God and how it can be affected, either for good or for weakness, by the way we think and way we do things. What these men did contributed positively to the service of God.

Nehemiah too was a man who was considering for the welfare of his people, and considering for Jerusalem. God put things into his heart; and that is where matters begin to work rightly as hearts are affected and something is stirred there that is not of man naturally but is begotten of God. May our hearts be stirred; may the word of God stir us and prompt us to act not as natural men would act, but in a way that is pleasurable to the heart of Christ. It just impresses one’s heart, as reading Scripture, what persons went through. It is what they went through in their time, but now it is your time and my time. The tests may be a little different, but yet they are really the same, as to how things affect God. We should be affected so that we act for God in matters and not for ourselves.

It is interesting as to these other persons that “it grieved them exceedingly that there had come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel”. They were on the side of the enemy, in the enemy’s camp. Well, may it grieve the enemy today to see persons who are prepared to stand for the rights of Christ, who have been brought to what God would have them brought to. It is not that we would seek anything against anyone, but we would stand for the rights of Christ. It will grieve the enemy. It may cause the enemy to rise up, but we must go through in relation to what is for God and move as Nehemiah did. He says, “I came to Jerusalem, and was there three days. And I arose in the night, I and some few men with me”.

Thank God for the togetherness that our brother referred to in the seven pillars. It is a needful thing in a local assembly. Maybe there are few men, maybe there are not seven in a locality. We were impressed on the other side with some localities with just two. “Two or three”, the Lord says (Matthew 18: 20), but thank God for the togetherness that there can be even in a local assembly with but few.

Nehemiah says, “I and some few men with me—but I told no man what my God had put in my heart to do”. Think of a man just having his own link with God in this way. It is beautiful, and it is available to you and to me to have a link with God and to have some such impress, and I think we will find that that impress links with the same impress in the heart of another.

It is the unison that God is looking for. It will lead to the building of the walls of Jerusalem and it will lead, I am sure, to the service of song. You get the service of song both in this book and in Ezra, these recovery books. We are in days of recovery and I am sure that as there is preparedness to commit ourselves there will be a strengthening to take up what needs to be taken up for the pleasure of our God, and to do it in a way that brings about blessing and a result for God’s glory. May it be so for His name’s sake.
A captured heart; O Lord may this be mine,
Held fast in that eternal love of Thine—
No more to taste the joys of things below,
No more the sorrows of those joys to know.
A captured heart; what else, Lord, can it be
If I am finding all my joy in Thee?
If in Thine own pure love alone I find
My all-sufficient food for heart and mind?
A captured heart! Thou gav’st Thyself for me
That I might even now be fully free
From all that kept me from Thy loving side,
Be free to worship Thee who for me died.
A captured heart! O Lord I now can feed
Upon Thyself—Thou meetest all my need;
My heart, which this world’s joys before had tried,
Now with Thyself for ever satisfied.
c. 1928, with Christ 19

‘FRIENDSHIP’ Christ has a circle of friends. It is not so large as the circle of those who know and trust Him as their Saviour. Whether I am among His friends can easily be tested by His own statement in John 15: 14—“Ye are my friends if ye practise whatever I command you”. Clearly if I am not practising what He commands I cannot claim to be among His friends. It is meant
to appeal to every lover of Christ; as loving Him we surely would want to be in the near circle of those who give Him comfort and pleasure because it is their desire and joy to do His will.

Knowing the kind of persons whom the Lord Jesus calls His friends will decide who are my friends. How can I have free and happy social links with those who are not in the circle of the friends of Jesus? If through grace it has become my main concern to please Him who loved me and gave Himself for me, how can my circle of friends include those to whom His commandments are of little importance? It is a happy thing—a right thing—when my friends are His friends according to John 15: 14. That is what John again speaks of—“The friends greet thee. Greet the friends by name”, 3 John 14; they are those who are, as he says, “walking in the truth” (3 John 4).

Two cannot walk together unless they be agreed; and, if we are faithful to the Lord, we shall find that it is impossible to maintain links of friendship with those in a path spiritually different from our own. This does not mean that we are to be ungracious or inaccessible to people. To be courteous is an exhortation to which we must give heed; but friendship implies, indeed it supposes, a mutuality and an intimacy and oneness quite impossible between two persons, one of whom is in the path of the will of God while the other is not. Let us again remind ourselves of the psalmist’s words, “I am a companion of all them that fear thee, and of them that keep thy precepts”, Psalm 119: 63 (A.V.).
